title: Chapter 5: Conclusions and Recommendations
author: Karylle Vinces J. Aliswag & Juana Mari A. Del Rosario

blocks.text: This study enhanced the Seeded Region Growing (SRG) algorithm of Adams and Bischof (1994) for the localization and delineation of brain tumors on two-dimensional contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI slices, with one enhancement for each specific objective, and evaluated the resulting Enhanced Seeded Region Growing (ESRG) algorithm against the original algorithm on a random sample of 600 test patients (300 glioma and 300 meningioma) from the BraTS 2023 dataset, after all parameters had been fixed on a separate development set. Both algorithms received the same slices, seeds, and parameter values, and the test set was evaluated once. The results are reported separately for glioma and meningioma. Based on the results in Chapter Four, the following conclusions are drawn.

First, automatic seed selection through Multi-Level Otsu Thresholding with connected-component filtering makes the segmentation reproducible and removes its dependence on where the operator clicks: repeated runs produced identical masks on every slice, whereas moving the planted seeds of the SRG by a few millimeters changed its DSC by at least 0.20 on 30.0% of glioma and 6.0% of meningioma slices. The automatic seed was placed inside the tumor on 85.0% of meningioma slices, with a lower confidence bound of 80.5% that meets the 70% target, but only on 58.3% of glioma slices (lower bound 52.7%). When the seed hit the tumor, the automatic ESRG reached a mean DSC of 0.609 for glioma and 0.833 for meningioma; when it missed, 0.028 and 0.061. The automatic DSC was nevertheless significantly lower than that of the planted placements in both tumor types. Objective 1 is therefore achieved for meningioma but not for glioma, for which the manual seeding option remains necessary.

Second, the local difference measure computed in the log domain did not, by itself, minimize undersegmentation in a way that improves the segmentation. Added to the original algorithm, it raised the median recall to 1.000 in both tumor types, but only because the region flooded the brain on 86.7% of glioma and 88.3% of meningioma slices, and the median DSC fell from 0.684 to 0.133 and from 0.931 to 0.137. Within the ESRG, where the stopping criterion bounds the region, the measure significantly increased recall (median 0.796 → 0.854) and DSC for meningioma, but not for glioma. Objective 2 is therefore met only in part: the measure reduces undersegmentation within the ESRG for meningioma, but it is not sufficient on its own and is useful only in combination with a stopping criterion.

Third, the stopping criterion that adapts to the intensity variability of the growing region, supported with a global drift guard, decreased boundary leakage in every comparison. Removed from the ESRG, its absence let the region flood the brain on 83.0% of glioma and 83.0% of meningioma slices and lowered the median DSC from 0.542 to 0.136 and from 0.865 to 0.173. From the tumor seed alone, it kept the original algorithm inside the tumor more strictly than two competing seeds did (median precision 0.991 → 1.000 for glioma and 0.955 → 0.998 for meningioma), but it also stopped the region before the whole tumor was covered, so the DSC was lower (median 0.684 → 0.320 and 0.931 → 0.802). Objective 3 is therefore met with respect to leakage, measured by precision, but not under the full decision rule, which also required a lower boundary distance and an unharmed DSC.

Fourth, the comparison of the two algorithms depends on the input the operator gives. With the same single planted tumor seed, the original algorithm has no competing region to stop it and absorbs the whole image (median DSC 0.023 for glioma and 0.015 for meningioma), whereas the ESRG stops at the tumor (0.562 for glioma and 0.876 for meningioma); the difference is large and significant in both tumor types. When the original algorithm also receives a healthy-tissue and a background seed, it obtains the higher DSC (median 0.684 for glioma and 0.931 for meningioma, against the ESRG’s values above), and the same holds when both algorithms start from the same automatic seed. The ESRG leaks less (higher precision) and needs only a single seed, or none, but it recovers less of the tumor (lower recall). It is also much faster, with a median processing time of 0.37 s for glioma and 0.54 s for meningioma with a planted seed against 5.89 s for glioma and 6.80 s for meningioma for the original algorithm with three seeds. The study therefore does not demonstrate an overall improvement in segmentation accuracy over the original algorithm supplied with competing seeds, but it does show that the ESRG delivers a controlled, fast, and reproducible segmentation from one seed where the original algorithm cannot.

Taken together, the enhancements are complementary rather than independent: the local log-domain measure lets the region reach the tumor boundary, and the stopping criterion keeps it from crossing it. Performance depended strongly on the tumor type: meningioma was delineated well without any user input (median DSC 0.866 with automatic seeding), whereas glioma, whose heterogeneous and infiltrative enhancement offers no sharp intensity boundary, remains the practical limit of the method (median DSC 0.265 with automatic seeding and 0.562 with a planted seed).

These conclusions are subject to the following limitations. The system operates on single two-dimensional slices of one MRI sequence and uses the tumor core as the reference standard, excluding edema. Only slices with a tumor core of at least 150 mm² were eligible, so small tumors and the thin upper and lower sections of a tumor were not evaluated. The planted seeds were placed by a simulated careful operator with knowledge of the ground truth, so seeds placed by real users may give lower scores, particularly for the original algorithm, which needs three correctly placed seeds. The images were skull-stripped by the dataset providers, which the brain mask of the system relies on. The processing times were measured with several slices running in parallel on one laptop, partly on battery power, and indicate relative speed only. The comparison at equal input and the comparison from the same automatic seed were added after the test run, using results already collected, and are descriptive. Finally, the decision to adopt the running global mean was made by the researchers although it did not meet the pre-set development-set acceptance margin; it was documented before the test set was opened.

Based on these findings, the following recommendations are offered. The system may be used as an assistive tool that gives clinicians and annotators a reproducible starting contour: with automatic seeding for well-circumscribed, enhancing tumors such as meningioma, and with the manual seeding option for gliomas. Because every stage of the method is interpretable, its contours can be reviewed and corrected by the user.

Future work should first improve the localization of gliomas by automatic seed selection, the stage that limited the fully automatic pipeline. Additional ranking cues, such as anatomical position, symmetry between the hemispheres, and texture, may separate the tumor from vessels and other enhancing structures, and the system may present the top-ranked candidates for one-click confirmation.

Second, because the ESRG errs toward undersegmentation while the original algorithm errs toward leakage, future work should combine their strengths: for example, by letting the stopping bounds relax gradually while the region remains compact, or by using competing regions, when the user supplies them, together with the adaptive stopping criterion. Any such change should be tuned on development data and confirmed on an independent test set, as in this study.

Finally, the method may be extended to multiple sequences, such as T2-weighted and FLAIR images, which delineate infiltrative tumors better than T1-CE alone; to three dimensions, by carrying the seed and region statistics across neighboring slices; and to clinical scans that have not been skull-stripped or bias-corrected. Its masks may also serve as initial contours for learning-based segmentation methods.
